title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 14: An Emerging Paradigm of Free Expression
keywords: An Emerging Paradigm of Free Expression
Article III, Section 4 of the Philippine Constitution
ABS-CBN Broadcasting Corporation v. Commission on Elections
World Association for Public Opinion Research (WAPOR)
the first recorded opinion survey in history
primary_topics: Chapter 14 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's address arguing that the public opinion poll is 'an emerging paradigm of free expression,' a new mode of protected speech whose growing role nurtures and strengthens Philippine democracy.

His survey of the constitutional architecture of free expression -- its two aspects of freedom from previous restraint and from subsequent punishment, its expansion from speech and print to flags, picket lines, film, cell phones and the Internet, and its standing as a preferred right.

His account of the two Philippine cases that placed polling inside that protection: ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll decision he wrote himself, and SWS v. Comelec, written by Justice Vicente V. Mendoza, striking down Section 5.4 of the Fair Elections Act.

His insistence that the freedom is not absolute but conditioned on responsibility -- reasonable regulation of how polls are conducted, transparency in methodology, and a duty on pollsters to educate the public about margins of error, sample size and the potential for abuse.
sub_topics: He opens with the Gospel reading of August 25, 2002, in which Jesus asks 'Who do people say that I am?' and then 'But who do you say that I am?', calling it 'the first recorded opinion survey in history' and evidence that polling is rooted in theology as well as law, before confining himself to the juridical bases.

He invokes the adage attributed to Voltaire -- 'I may not agree with what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it' -- as capturing the essence of a right that keeps government in check and prevents tyranny.

He sets out the two aspects of free expression: freedom from previous restraint or censorship under Section 4 of Article III, and freedom from subsequent punishment under Section 18, and notes the cluster of rights it carries, including the right to be silent, to listen and not to listen.

He traces the widening modes of expression from speech, sermons, slogans, graffiti and plays, to flags, caricatures, floats, yellow ribbons, clenched fists and silent picket lines, to movies, radio, cell phones, satellites and the Internet, and says he awaits the day the Internet's constitutional protection reaches the judiciary.

He defines a public opinion poll as a survey to determine the opinion of the public or a segment of it, used to measure support for or against government as well as commercially, and argues that poll results both reflect and shape people's views and give voters power through information.

He cites Dr. Mahar Mangahas's WAPOR keynote that polls help electorates acquire and maintain genuine political power, and that a government without means of measuring popular information is ineffective.

He compares foreign practice: Singapore bans election and exit polls; the Supreme Court of India in 1999 dismissed the Election Commission's petition to ban publication of pre-election and exit polls for the 13th Lok Sabha elections; Mexico criminalizes releasing a predictive poll within eight days of an election; France prohibits publication immediately before; the United Kingdom relies on voluntary restraint.
He notes the multiple-time-zone problem, recalling the premature and inaccurate call for Gore in Florida before Midwest and West polls had closed.

He recounts ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the decision he 'had the honor of writing,' which defined exit polls and answered with 'a firm No' the question whether Comelec could totally prohibit them and the dissemination of their results.

He restates the decision's account of freedom of expression as a fundamental principle and preferred right, an indispensable condition of nearly every other freedom, committed to debate that is 'uninhibited, robust and wide open,' and encompassing, after Holmes, 'the thought we hate, no less than the thought we agree with.'

He lays out the two tests for restrictions -- the clear and present danger rule as explained by Holmes, with the false shout of 'Fire, fire' in a crowded theater, and the dangerous tendency rule as explained by Justice Felix Bautista Angelo in Cabansag v. Fernandez and applied in People v. Perez to seditious words against Wood.

He reports that the present Court adheres to the more liberal clear and present danger rule, that restraints should be 'greeted with furrowed brows,' and that the presumption runs against the validity of prior censorship.

He rehearses the Court's answers to Comelec's claim that exit polls sow confusion and endanger electoral credibility: interviewees are randomly selected precisely to be representative, the survey does not replace or stand on a par with the official count, and an election is an exercise separate from and unaffected by the poll.

He adds the caution that while all polling organizations have an equal right to publicize surveys, they do not enjoy equal public credibility -- just as newspapers and broadcasters do not enjoy equal acceptability.

He recounts his elation at SWS v. Comelec, written by Justice Mendoza, who had dissented in the earlier case, striking down Section 5.4 of RA 9006, which banned publication of election surveys fifteen days before a national and seven days before a local election.

He sets out the Court's three grounds: the ban was a prior restraint; Comelec's constitutional power under Article IX-C, Section 4 extends only to equal opportunity, time, space and right to reply and reasonable rates; and the provision failed the third and fourth criteria of United States v. O'Brien.

He explains the O'Brien failures: the governmental interest was 'not unrelated to the suppression of free expression' since it suppressed a whole class of expression while letting commentators speak, showing a bias for personal opinion over statistical results; and the aims of preventing last-minute pressure, bandwagon effects, the junking of weak candidates and dagdag-bawas could be met by other means.

He recalls his own Concurring Opinion reiterating that free expression is a preferred right whose limitation requires a clear and present danger of substantive character, and that Comelec failed to convince him any such danger was 'lurking and threatening to explode.'

He concedes that polling, like any right, may be reasonably regulated -- not to stifle it but to safeguard it -- and repeats ABS-CBN's recommendations: a limited designated area, professional survey groups only, a reasonable distance from voting centers, distinctive clothing, and informed consent with confidentiality.

He closes on freedom and responsibility: polls are open to abuse for partisan ends, so pollsters must publish explanations of margin of error, sample size and demographics, be transparent in methodology, and educate the public on both the advantages and the limitations of polling.

stances.claim: The public opinion poll is a genuine mode of free expression -- 'an emerging paradigm' of it -- and properly understood, polling goes into the very essence of that freedom.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional expansion -- tracing the widening forms of expression from speech to picket lines to the Internet, then placing polling in that line

stances.claim: Comelec could not totally prohibit exit polls or the dissemination of their results, because its fears were speculative and exit polls create no obvious or imminent risk that circumspect governance could not prevent.
stances.rhetorical_move: point-by-point rebuttal of the Comelec's confusion, unreliability and integrity arguments, grounded in the decision he himself penned

stances.claim: Freedom of expression is a preferred right standing higher than substantive economic freedom, so any limitation must be justified by a clear and present danger of substantive character, and the presumption runs against prior censorship.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal ranking -- contrasting the clear and present danger rule with the older dangerous tendency rule and aligning the present Court with the former

stances.claim: If journalists and broadcasters may disseminate their individual opinion, there is no reason to ban publication of polls that reflect the views of the general population; banning them shows a bias for personal opinion over statistical results.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from parity -- an a fortiori comparison between commentators and pollsters

stances.claim: For every freedom there is a corresponding responsibility: polling may be reasonably regulated to safeguard rather than stifle it, and pollsters owe the public transparency in methodology and education about margin of error, sample size and the potential for abuse.
stances.rhetorical_move: balancing coda -- conceding the risk of partisan abuse and converting it into a duty on the poll-takers rather than a power in the state

notable_anecdotes: The first opinion survey: he opens by reading the August 25, 2002 Gospel, in which Jesus asks his disciples what people say of him and then what they themselves say, and calls it the first recorded opinion survey in history.

Writing the exit-poll decision: he notes that the definition of exit polls came from 'the Decision that I had the honor of writing' in ABS-CBN v. Comelec, which answered Comelec's claimed power with a firm 'No.'
His elation at SWS: he recalls being pleased not only by the SWS ruling but by the fact that its writer, Justice Mendoza, had dissented in the earlier exit-poll case he had penned.
Waiting for the Internet case: he says he is 'eagerly waiting for the day' when the issues on the Internet's constitutional protection come before the judiciary for resolution.

The unconvinced concurrer: in his Concurring Opinion in SWS he wrote that Comelec had failed to convince him that any substantive danger was lurking and threatening to explode if ignited by the prohibited surveys.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 14 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced CJP's address contending that the public opinion poll is an emerging paradigm of free expression. He opened with the Gospel reading of August 25, 2002, in which Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was and then who they themselves said he was, calling it 'the first recorded opinion survey in history' and evidence that 'polling is rooted not only in law, but also in theology,' before confining himself to juridical grounds. Invoking the adage attributed to Voltaire, he set out the two aspects of free expression -- freedom from previous restraint under Section 4 of Article III and freedom from subsequent punishment under Section 18 -- and traced the widening modes of expression from sermons and slogans to yellow ribbons and silent picket lines to satellites and the Internet, whose constitutional protection he said he awaited. He argued that polls both reflect and shape opinion and arm voters with power, citing Mahar Mangahas's WAPOR keynote, and compared foreign regimes in Singapore, India, Mexico, France, the United Kingdom and the United States, including the premature Florida call. He then recounted ABS-CBN v. Comelec, the exit-poll decision he wrote, which held that Comelec could not prohibit exit polls, restating the Court's account of expression as a preferred right embracing 'the thought we hate, no less than the thought we agree with,' the clear and present danger rule of Holmes against the dangerous tendency rule of Cabansag v. Fernandez and People v. Perez, and the Court's rebuttals of Comelec's claims of confusion and unreliability. He then welcomed SWS v. Comelec, written by Justice Mendoza, which struck down Section 5.4 of the Fair Elections Act as a prior restraint beyond Comelec's Article IX-C powers and failing the third and fourth O'Brien criteria, and recalled his own Concurring Opinion that no substantive danger had been shown. He closed by conceding that polling may be reasonably regulated to safeguard it, endorsing the ABS-CBN recommendations on how exit polls should be conducted, and insisting that 'For every freedom, there is a corresponding responsibility,' with pollsters bound to disclose methodology and educate the public on the limits and abuses of polls.
